news.headline: ‘AI speeding up drug design; next step is faster, cheaper medicines’: Siddhartha Mukherjee at HT Leadership Summit
news.story_lead: ‘AI speeding up drug design; next step is faster, cheaper medicines’: Siddhartha Mukherjee at HT Leadership Summit He urged safeguards for faster trials and said India has a historic opportunity to make medicines faster, cheaper and better. Artificial intelligence is already cutting the time it takes to design new medicines from years to months, oncologist and author Siddhartha Mukherjee said on Saturday, but it must now make medicines faster, cheaper and better for patients if it is to prove its worth. “The single mitigating feature of AI is its capacity to produce transformative medicine,” Mukherjee, co-founder and chief executive of the drug-discovery company Manas AI, said at the 24th edition of the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit.
news.full_article_text: ‘AI speeding up drug design; next step is faster, cheaper medicines’: Siddhartha Mukherjee at HT Leadership Summit He urged safeguards for faster trials and said India has a historic opportunity to make medicines faster, cheaper and better. Artificial intelligence is already cutting the time it takes to design new medicines from years to months, oncologist and author Siddhartha Mukherjee said on Saturday, but it must now make medicines faster, cheaper and better for patients if it is to prove its worth. “The single mitigating feature of AI is its capacity to produce transformative medicine,” Mukherjee, co-founder and chief executive of the drug-discovery company Manas AI, said at the 24th edition of the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit. “Exhibit A of AI’s transformative power for human good is medicine. And if we fail in exhibit A, that creates an enormous problem for… whether we put up data centres or not, or what the value is of AI in various other industries.” The harder part, he said, is what happens after a molecule is designed: testing it in people and getting it approved, which have barely changed. AI could speed up clinical trials too, he said, but only with safeguards, so that medicines that do not work are not released to patients. India, he said, has a “historic opportunity” to show what AI can deliver if it reforms how new drugs are tested and approved. To lay out his case, Mukherjee explained how arduous drug discovery can be. Every medicine binds to a protein in the body, the way a key fits a lock, he explained. There are 10 to the power of 24 possible small-molecule keys, far too many to try one by one, so modern drug design starts with the lock: find a “keyhole” in the target protein, then build a molecule from scratch to fit it. Also Read | Remarkable progress, but cancer won't be cured in the near future: Siddhartha Mukherjee at HTLS This is where AI comes in, he said, citing his company Manas, which combines AI, “which is a neural system”, with what it calls “medicinal intelligence”: “the rules of physics and chemistry”. Illustrating how the technology can compress timelines for drug discovery, he cited the case of daraxonrasib, a pancreatic cancer drug. “It took a human researcher about ten years to find that keyhole,” Mukherjee said, adding: “It took our algorithm two hours to find that same keyhole.” That gain, he said, came “just from the keyhole finding module”. Manas sends 50 to 100 compounds at a time to Chinese chemical companies, which return test data in about three weeks. One molecule for a particular cancer, he said, “was generated completely without human intervention” and is “about two hundred times more potent than the competitor medicine that is available in the market”. Such work once took seven to eight years, he said; it now takes three to four months. “But the back end, which is where we actually put these molecules into humans and test them against diseases, is still very much the same,” he said. “More medicines are emerging very rapidly from our engines, and then they’re getting blocked at the pinch point.” AI does not change what he called the “phase two coin flip”, the chance that a drug fails in mid-stage trials. Also Read | ‘Every cancer is different’: Manas AI's CEO Siddhartha Mukherjee on the search for a cure |HTLS 2026 In a Q&A with HT’s R Sukumar, Mukherjee was asked whether medicine was “too hung up on the accepted model of clinical testing”, and if there is a case to radically overhaul that, given the computing power AI now offers. “Well, the quick answer is, yes, of course, there’s a radical way to change it,” Mukherjee said, but added that the question was whether it should be changed. Medicine invented the randomised, blinded clinical trial “essentially to overcome human bias”, he said. “We want to see our medicine succeed.” Trials could be sped up by using historical or simulated data as the comparison group, he said, but he warned of “BIBO, bias in, bias out”. Relying on such data alone, he said, risks “unleashing medicines into the world which actually don’t work or don’t work as well as we think they do”. He suggested conditional approval, which he said the Europeans are trying “quite a lot”: a medicine is approved after a rapid trial, the trial continues with proper controls, and the approval can be withdrawn after two or three years. He called India’s chance to change the economics of medicine the punchline of his talk. “Of all countries in the world, China and I truly believe India, with appropriate regulatory and technological reform,” can reverse a long trend in which, he said, the “number of medicines approved over time has actually been decreasing… and the cost of each medicine has been increasing”. “We have a historic opportunity in this country,” he said. India can make the difference in testing, he said, “because we have a highly educated population of physicians, physician scientists”. He cited Immuneel, a Bengaluru cell-therapy company he said he launched about three years ago with Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw. Its therapy for blood cancers first used binders borrowed from other countries. “But for the first time, we have created a synthetic binder using AI,” he said. He described the new molecules, made with Manas, as “first in class, first in kind, made in India”. Also Read | Medicine is AI’s real test, and India has a historic opportunity: Siddhartha Mukherjee “The medicine that costs $500,000 in the United States is now being sold. It’s now a commercial product, is being sold for $35,000 in India,” he said. “The human resources and the human capital which is present here is really the answer,” he said, to speeding up what he called “the second half of the equation”. He closed his talk where he began: “If it’s not true that medicines become faster, cheaper, better, then we have failed the AI revolution.” Mukherjee, born in New Delhi and trained at Stanford, Oxford and Harvard, is on leave from Columbia University’s medical faculty. He won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for The Emperor of All Maladies, his history of cancer. - Artificial Intelligence

news.headline: 25 shops gutted in fire at woollens market in Gurugram's Pataudi, no injuries reported
news.story_lead: 25 shops gutted in fire at woollens market in Gurugram's Pataudi, no injuries reported Firefighters brought the blaze under control, with no injuries reported. The cause and extent of the damage remain unknown. Around 25 shops were completely burned down on Sunday morning after a fire broke out here in the woollens market at the Ramlila Ground in Gurugram's Pataudi town, a fire officer said.

Fire personnel brought the blaze under control after a strenuous effort. No injuries have been reported in this incident, he added. An official said that a woman in the area heard a noise at around 4 am and discovered that the market was on fire. She alerted others, but by then, the blaze had become massive. Local residents said that every year, from November to February, a woollens market is set up on the eastern part of Ramlila Maidan in Pataudi. This year, it opened on November 4, under the aegis of the Himalayan Tribal Trade Association, and featured stalls run by vendors from Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir. news.headline: India-Canada free trade deal may be concluded next month, says Maninder Sidhu
news.story_lead: India-Canada free trade deal may be concluded next month, says Maninder Sidhu Canada’s Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said India could be the next free trade deal concluded as CEPA negotiations target a December deadline. Toronto: After Ottawa announced the successful conclusion of negotiations towards a free trade agreement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations or ASEAN and the Philippines, Canada’s Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu expressed confidence that India will be “the next one that we’re going to get done.” That reference was to ongoing negotiations towards the comprehensive economic partnership agreement or CEPA. Sidhu travelled to India for three days last week as the sixth round of negotiations commenced.
news.full_article_text: India-Canada free trade deal may be concluded next month, says Maninder Sidhu Canada’s Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said India could be the next free trade deal concluded as CEPA negotiations target a December deadline. Toronto: After Ottawa announced the successful conclusion of negotiations towards a free trade agreement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations or ASEAN and the Philippines, Canada’s Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu expressed confidence that India will be “the next one that we’re going to get done.” That reference was to ongoing negotiations towards the comprehensive economic partnership agreement or CEPA. Sidhu travelled to India for three days last week as the sixth round of negotiations commenced. “India will be the next one that we’re going to get done,” he told reporters in Manila, where he was accompanying Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to the ASEAN Summit. Sidhu travelled to Manila from India, where he spent three days and held a bilateral meeting with Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal in New Delhi. Sidhu expressed optimism that the two countries would be able to “lock down” the agreement by next month, the deadline set by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Carney for concluding negotiations. Modi is scheduled to visit Canada in the second week of December, with the focus being on announcing the conclusion of the free trade agreement talks. Sidhu stressed that in looking at the deal with India, Canada wasn’t just throwing a dart at a board, but had consulted with businesses, companies and chambers of commerce over the markets to which they sought access. In India, Sidhu also participated in the Confederation of Indian Industry or CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam, which a statement from Global Affairs Canada said “reinforced Canada’s commitment to diversifying its commercial relationships with international partners and creating new opportunities for Canadian businesses and workers.” The objective of the CEPA is to double bilateral trade to CA$ 70 billion by 2030. “With a market of nearly 1.5 billion people, India presents significant opportunities for Canadian businesses across a range of sectors, from agri-food and clean energy to AI and aerospace. Canada is a trusted and reliable partner, and building closer economic ties with India will help create better jobs here at home,” Sidhu said in the statement.

news.story_lead: My real mission is to see Tricolour on Moon by 2040: Captain Shubhanshu Shukla Shukla said he never felt alone during Axiom Mission 4 that took him to space and back in June 2025, "because the whole nation was part of the mission". news.full_article_text: My real mission is to see Tricolour on Moon by 2040: Captain Shubhanshu Shukla Shukla said he never felt alone during Axiom Mission 4 that took him to space and back in June 2025, "because the whole nation was part of the mission". Captain Shubhanshu Shukla, the first Indian astronaut to visit the International Space Station, said on Saturday that his real mission was to see a fellow Indian plant the Tricolour on the Moon by 2040. He said he never felt alone during Axiom Mission 4 that took him to space and back in June 2025, "because the whole nation was part of the mission". Talking during a session at the 10th Military Literature Festival here, the internationally recognised astronaut said, "After Axiom, I am actively engaged in preparing our national mission Gaganyaan to succeed and further contribute to India's growth and prosperity." During the session, titled "From Fighter Cockpit to Spacecraft: India's New Frontier in Air and Space Power", Shukla delivered a presentation of his 20-days-and-3-hours-long journey to space. Sharing his experience, he said taking off from the International Space Station (ISS) on the Space Capsule was "violent and chaotic", contrary to his expectations. "As we lifted off from the ISS, a doubt crossed my mind whether I had made the right decision to travel to space," he said, adding that initial anxiety and confusion are in-built in any challenge. Urging youngsters to take up science and follow their dreams with courage, he said classrooms foster audacious dreams, which should be nurtured with courage and spirit for one to succeed and serve society. Sharing his in-flight experience of staying in a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for over 20 days, he said the loss of gravity makes one feel awkward at first. "You grow taller in size; your heart becomes smaller. There are numerous physical and mental changes you feel while in space. Though you prepare for each challenge, the real power comes to you from your conviction to go back and serve society through research," he added. Motivating youngsters to take up challenges in the right spirit, Shukla said Mission Director Dr Peggy Whitson had endured nine rejections before being chosen to fly to space at the age of 39. "The fact that Dr Whitson now has the longest stay in space is motivation to all those feeling negative at any stage in their life," he added. In another session on the second day of the MLF, subject experts said India needs an effective and regular assessment of its national security needs and aspirations. With China far ahead even of the US, the world order is rapidly imploding, with leading global powers expending military energies in pursuits ranging from objectives of territory gain, to securing oil reserves, to regime change, they said during a panel discussion on "Turbulent World Order: Where India Stands". This culminates in the urgent need for India to review and fortify its security architecture through innovations in space, cyber and Artificial Intelligence, they said. Sharing his thoughts during the discussion, strategic affairs expert Sushant Sareen said there is nothing called "strategic dependence" and that, at most, it is just a euphemism. "Even the US is dependent upon so many other countries for making up its needs and aspirations. No nation can be fully dependent upon any one country. We need to outgrow this perception as each country today prioritises its own needs," Sareen said. Referring to the impact of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars on equations between old partner nations, Sareen said there is bound to be some resistance, which may not eventually result in a major alliance in Europe. Adding a distinctive educational dimension, Defence Studies students of Government College, Sector 11, Chandigarh, presented "Saga of Courage and Bravery", bringing India's military heritage, valour and traditions of sacrifice into focus. The festival also featured the Clarion Call Theatre's war films, cultural performances, weapons display, military paintings, philately and vintage automobiles, the statement said. The Military Literature Festival is a joint initiative of the Punjab government, Chandigarh administration and Western Command Headquarters at Chandimandir.

A girl aged about 18 climbed a mobile tower in Baithwalia village of Uttar Pradesh's Maharajganj district on Sunday morning, insisting that she be allowed to marry her boyfriend, police said. The girl threatened to jump off the tower if her family refused to accept her demand, triggering panic among her family members and drawing a large crowd to the spot.

news.headline: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
news.story_lead: Watch: US ground stop caused by issue during copper wire update, transport secretary says - Published 14 November 2026, 03:10 GMT An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks. Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday. US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.
news.full_article_text: Watch: US ground stop caused by issue during copper wire update, transport secretary says - Published 14 November 2026, 03:10 GMT An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks. Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday. US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers. Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe. Here's what we know. What caused the stoppage? On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network. According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper. This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted. As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned". He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper." Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag. In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel. "You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said "You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added. A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel". He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." How many flights were affected? The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware. The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations. Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport. The FAA opened skies again at 20:15 EST. - Have you been affected by the flight disruption? Get in touch 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop What about international flights? All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended. There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco. Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning. A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport. Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned. Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada. When will normal service resume? Duffy said on Saturday: "We are back at full operations." But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened. FlightAware said more than 3,500 flights in the US were cancelled while 2,000 were delayed. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys. Meanwhile, JetBlue cancelled 40% of its scheduled journeys. Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport What are your rights? In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness. As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems. But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly. It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund. In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers. Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe. Here's what we know. What caused the stoppage? On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network. According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper. This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted. As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned". He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper." Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag. In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel. "You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said "You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added. A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel". He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." How many flights were affected? The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations. Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport. news.headline: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
news.story_lead: Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New Orleans - Published 13 November 2026 Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker. The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt. The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for.
news.full_article_text: Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New Orleans - Published 13 November 2026 Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker. The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt. The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi". The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering." New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference on Friday that all credit in the rescue effort should go to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help". "We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said. Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference. - Were you in the area at the time of incident? Get in touch . There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority. Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side, Moreno said. Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort. The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway. On Saturday, Moreno said that nine people are still in hospital. She said that the captain of the ship was injured in the accident but refused medical treatment until he knew all passengers and crew were accounted for. US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue had been an "incredible job". Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued. Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what had occurred. Still covered in dirt from the boat crash, Joe Knab of Kansas told New Orleans NBC affiliate WDSU that the ship quickly capsized after the collision. He spent about 20 minutes in the water before being rescued. "When we first went in we were bobbing underneath the water; it was sinking pretty fast, but we finally got out of there," he said. Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he had seen the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision. "It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic." Holford added that he had seen passengers and crew "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking. The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website. news.story_lead: - Published 14 November 2026, 10:30 GMT US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties". news.full_article_text: - Published 14 November 2026, 10:30 GMT US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties". The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory. "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday. He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow. Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. news.headline: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
news.story_lead: Watch: US ground stop caused by issue during copper wire update, transport secretary says - Published 14 November 2026, 08:42 GMT A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment. The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.
news.full_article_text: Watch: US ground stop caused by issue during copper wire update, transport secretary says - Published 14 November 2026, 08:42 GMT A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment. The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said. Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days. Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said. The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said. The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons. Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related." On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday. More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues. In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space. Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks. news.full_article_text:
### Seat Negotiations and Major Governance Developments in Uttar Pradesh

In a significant political disclosure, Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav revealed that the Congress party had requested 181 seats during seat-sharing discussions. This marks the first public confirmation of the specific number of seats sought by Congress in coalition talks.

### Key Policy, Evaluation, and Election Administrative Updates

- **Impact of Smartphone & Tablet Scheme**: A study conducted by the Indian Institute of Management Lucknow (IIM-L) revealed that the Uttar Pradesh government's free smartphone and tablet distribution scheme has successfully benefited 3 crore (30 million) individuals across the state.
- **Homeless Count under Census 2027**: As part of the preliminary operations for Census 2027, Uttar Pradesh authorities will conduct a targeted headcount of homeless individuals on the night of January 4.
- **EVM Demonstration Centers**: To enhance voter awareness, Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) demonstration centers are scheduled to open across all districts of Uttar Pradesh starting November 20.
- **Voter Roll Accuracy**: Administrative strictness has been announced regarding electoral roll updating; Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and officials may face deduction or forfeiture of their honorarium if voter rolls contain errors.
- **Skill Development Focus**: Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to address and spotlight skill development programs during a major event in Lucknow on November 21.
- **Regulatory Actions**: State authorities have initiated enforcement drives, taking action against 20 pollution testing centers for violating operational norms, while also seeking strict regulatory restrictions on the illicit diversion of codeine-based cough syrups.

hindi_translation.full_article_text:
### उत्तर प्रदेश में सीट बंटवारे और प्रमुख प्रशासनिक अपडेट

एक महत्वपूर्ण राजनीतिक खुलासे में, समाजवादी पार्टी (सपा) प्रमुख अखिलेश यादव ने बताया कि कांग्रेस पार्टी ने गठबंधन वार्ता के दौरान 181 सीटों की मांग की थी। यह पहला मौका है जब कांग्रेस द्वारा मांगी गई सीटों की संख्या की आधिकारिक पुष्टि हुई है।

### प्रमुख नीतिगत, मूल्यांकन और निर्वाचन प्रशासनिक अपडेट

- **स्मार्टफोन और टैबलेट योजना का प्रभाव**: भारतीय प्रबंध संस्थान लखनऊ (IIM-L) के एक अध्ययन से पता चला है कि उत्तर प्रदेश सरकार की मुफ्त स्मार्टफोन और टैबलेट वितरण योजना से राज्य भर में 3 करोड़ लोगों को लाभ हुआ है।
- **जनगणना 2027 के तहत बेघरों की गिनती**: जनगणना 2027 की शुरुआती तैयारियों के तहत, उत्तर प्रदेश प्रशासन 4 जनवरी की रात को बेघर लोगों की विशेष गिनती करेगा।
- **ईवीएम प्रदर्शन केंद्र**: मतदाताओं को जागरूक करने के लिए 20 नवंबर से उत्तर प्रदेश के सभी जिलों में इलेक्ट्रॉनिक वोटिंग मशीन (EVM) प्रदर्शन केंद्र खोले जाएंगे।
- **मतदाता सूची की शुद्धता**: मतदाता सूची के नवीनीकरण में त्रुटियों को लेकर कड़ा रुख अपनाया गया है; मतदाता सूची में गड़बड़ी पाए जाने पर बूथ लेवल अधिकारियों (BLO) और संबंधित अधिकारियों का मानदेय रोका जा सकता है।
- **कौशल विकास पर जोर**: प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी 21 नवंबर को लखनऊ में आयोजित एक कार्यक्रम के दौरान कौशल विकास पहलों पर विशेष ध्यान केंद्रित करेंगे।
- **नियामक कार्रवाई**: मानक का उल्लंघन करने पर उत्तर प्रदेश में 20 प्रदूषण जांच केंद्रों पर कार्रवाई की गई है, जबकि कोडीन युक्त कफ सिरप के अवैध इस्तेमाल पर सख्त पाबंदी लगाने की मांग की गई है।

* **वैश्विक सांस्कृतिक प्रभाव:** इस एकत्रीकरण ने वैश्विक स्तर पर लोकप्रिय संस्कृति पर फिल्म फ्रेंचाइजी के निरंतर प्रभाव को उजागर किया।

news.headline: NGT Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava Emphasises India's Role in Global Environmental Jurisprudence at COP17 in Armenia
news.story_lead: National Green Tribunal (NGT) Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava highlighted India's key contributions to global environmental jurisprudence during the COP17 conference held in Armenia. The address underscored India's dedicated judicial mechanisms and legal frameworks for environmental protection and sustainable governance on an international platform.
news.full_article_text:
### Overview of the Address
National Green Tribunal (NGT) Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava represented India at the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) hosted in Armenia, detailing the country's significant role in shaping international environmental jurisprudence.

### Key Factual Highlights
- **International Legal Representation:** NGT Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava presented India's judicial perspective on ecological conservation and legal accountability at the COP17 summit in Armenia.
- **Focus on Environmental Jurisprudence:** The address emphasized the impact of Indian legal frameworks, judicial precedents, and statutory environmental courts on global standards of environmental governance.
- **Role of the National Green Tribunal:** The presentation showcased the institutional framework of specialized bodies like the NGT in expediting environmental dispute resolution and enforcing compliance.
bullet_points: NGT Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava represented India at the COP17 conference in Armenia.
The address highlighted India's major contributions to global environmental jurisprudence.
Deliberation focused on Indian judicial mechanisms for environmental protection and climate justice.
Emphasised the importance of specialized legal bodies like the NGT in resolving environmental disputes efficiently.
Showcased India's legal commitment to balancing economic growth with ecological sustainability.
key_facts: Dignitary: Justice Prakash Shrivastava, Chairperson of the National Green Tribunal (NGT).
Event: 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17).
Venue Location: Armenia.
Core Theme: India's contributions to global environmental jurisprudence.
important_dates: November 14, 2026: Address delivered/reported at COP17 in Armenia.
exam_relevance: Prelims: Statutory nature of NGT, provisions under NGT Act 2010, and global environmental conventions (COP17 venue).
Mains: Role of judiciary in environmental governance, environmental jurisprudence in India, and functioning of specialized tribunals.
news.upsc_analysis: India's active participation in international forums such as COP17 highlights the growing global recognition of its environmental legal framework. The National Green Tribunal serves as a vital institutional model for specialized environmental adjudication, offering insights into how statutory bodies can strengthen ecological protection alongside economic development.
causes: Participation in the international COP17 conference in Armenia to share perspectives on environmental law and judicial governance.
impacts: Strengthens India's reputation in international environmental law and highlights the efficacy of its specialized tribunal system.
government_steps: Establishment of the National Green Tribunal under the NGT Act 2010 for specialized and speedy disposal of environmental cases.
constitutional_or_policy_link: Article 21: Right to a healthy environment interpreted as part of the Right to Life.
Article 48A: Directive Principle mandating the State to protect and improve the environment.
Article 51A(g): Fundamental Duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment.
way_forward: Enhance international judicial dialogue to standardize best practices in environmental law enforcement.
Strengthen institutional support for environmental tribunals to maintain swift dispute resolution.
news.mains_notes: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) plays a central role in India's environmental legal framework. Established under the NGT Act 2010, it handles complex environmental cases using judicial and expert members. Showcasing India's legal practices at global events like COP17 in Armenia underscores the relevance of specialized environmental courts in furthering international ecological governance.
mains_questions: Examine the role of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) in advancing environmental jurisprudence in India and its significance on global platforms.
Discuss how judicial activism and specialized tribunals contribute to achieving sustainable development goals while safeguarding constitutional environmental rights.

hindi_translation.story_lead: राष्ट्रीय हरित अधिकरण (NGT) के अध्यक्ष न्यायमूर्ति प्रकाश श्रीवास्तव ने आर्मेनिया में आयोजित कॉप17 सम्मेलन के दौरान वैश्विक पर्यावरणीय न्यायशास्त्र में भारत के महत्वपूर्ण योगदान को रेखांकित किया। उनके संबोधन ने पर्यावरण संरक्षण और सतत विकास के लिए समर्पित भारत के न्यायिक तंत्र को अंतरराष्ट्रीय मंच पर प्रस्तुत किया।
hindi_translation.full_article_text:
### संबोधन का अवलोकन
राष्ट्रीय हरित अधिकरण (NGT) के अध्यक्ष न्यायमूर्ति प्रकाश श्रीवास्तव ने आर्मेनिया में आयोजित 17वें कॉन्फ्रेंस ऑफ द पार्टीज (COP17) को संबोधित करते हुए वैश्विक पर्यावरणीय न्यायशास्त्र को आकार देने में भारत की महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका पर प्रकाश डाला।

### प्रमुख बातें
- **अंतरराष्ट्रीय प्रतिनिधित्व:** एनजीटी अध्यक्ष न्यायमूर्ति प्रकाश श्रीवास्तव ने आर्मेनिया में आयोजित कॉप17 बैठक में पर्यावरण संरक्षण और कानूनी जवाबदेही पर भारत के न्यायिक दृष्टिकोण का प्रतिनिधित्व किया।
- **पर्यावरणीय न्यायशास्त्र:** संबोधन में इस बात पर ध्यान केंद्रित किया गया कि भारत का कानूनी ढांचा, पर्यावरणीय अधिकरण और न्यायिक निर्णय वैश्विक पर्यावरणीय मानदंडों को आकार देने में किस प्रकार योगदान देते हैं।
- **राष्ट्रीय हरित अधिकरण की भूमिका:** प्रस्तुति ने त्वरित पर्यावरणीय न्याय देने और पारिस्थितिक अनुपालन सुनिश्चित करने में एनजीटी जैसे विशेष निकायों की संस्थागत मजबूती पर बल दिया।
bullet_points: एनजीटी अध्यक्ष न्यायमूर्ति प्रकाश श्रीवास्तव ने आर्मेनिया में कॉप17 सम्मेलन में भारत का प्रतिनिधित्व किया।
संबोधन में वैश्विक पर्यावरणीय न्यायशास्त्र में भारत के प्रमुख योगदान पर प्रकाश डाला गया।
पर्यावरण संरक्षण और जलवायु न्याय के लिए भारतीय न्यायिक तंत्र पर ध्यान केंद्रित किया गया।
पर्यावरण विवादों को कुशलतापूर्वक हल करने में एनजीटी जैसे विशेष निकायों के महत्व पर बल दिया।
पर्यावरण संरक्षण के साथ आर्थिक विकास को संतुलित करने की भारत की कानूनी प्रतिबद्धता को प्रदर्शित किया।
